title: The Great Vowel Shift
hook: Why English spells "bite" and "meet" so unlike the rest of Europe.
peek: Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English slid to new positions. Spelling was settling down at the same time, so English kept the old spellings with the new sounds, which is why its vowels look so odd to other Europeans.
lede: In Chaucer's time, "bite" sounded close to modern "beet", "meet" was nearer to "mate", and "house" was close to "hoose". Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English moved, each one pushing into the space of another. Linguists call it the Great Vowel Shift, and it is the main reason English spelling and pronunciation part ways.

bullets.text: The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen gave the change its name in the early twentieth century. He described it as a chain: as one vowel moved up, the vowel behind it moved up to fill the gap.

Nobody knows for sure. Ideas include people moving into London from other regions and the social pull of copying higher-status speech. Linguists still debate both the cause and how orderly it really was.
Printing arrived in England in the 1470s, and printers began fixing spellings while the shift was still under way. So English kept writing the old vowels long after people stopped saying them.

Shakespeare wrote near the end of the shift, and vowels have kept moving since, so some of his rhymes look broken today. Productions in reconstructed pronunciation, including some at London's rebuilt Globe theatre, bring those rhymes back.
The shift did not reach every dialect in the same way. In Scots, the old long vowel of "house" and "out" never moved, which is why "hoose" and "oot" still sound the way Chaucer might have said them.
